topic: Angular kinematics and moment of inertia
title: Angular variables and inertia
lede: Rotation swaps x, v, a for theta, omega, alpha — and adds a new inertia that depends on where the mass sits.

cards.heading: Angular variables
cards.body: Rotation trades linear variables for angular ones: angle theta in radians, angular velocity omega, angular acceleration alpha. Every constant-acceleration kinematics equation has an exact rotational twin — swap x for theta, v for omega, a for alpha — so there is nothing new to memorize. Angles in radians make the swap work cleanly, which is why radians are the default unit.

cards.heading: Moment of inertia
cards.body: Moment of inertia I measures how hard it is to spin an object up, and unlike mass it depends on where the mass sits — each bit counts as mr squared, so mass far from the axis matters much more. Point masses add directly, standard shapes have table values: hoop MR^2, disk (1/2)MR^2, rod about its center (1/12)ML^2, solid sphere (2/5)MR^2. The parallel-axis theorem moves the axis: I = I_cm + Md^2.
cards.math: I = \sum m_i r_i^2, \quad I = I_{\text{cm}} + Md^2

cards.heading: Worked example
cards.body: Two 3.0 kg masses sit at the ends of a light 2.0 m rod. About the center, each mass is 1.0 m from the axis, so I = (3.0)(1.0)^2 + (3.0)(1.0)^2 = 6.0 kg m^2. Now shift the axis to one end. Parallel axis with M = 6.0 kg and d = 1.0 m gives 6.0 + (6.0)(1.0)^2 = 12 kg m^2. Computing directly agrees: the near mass sits on the axis and contributes 0, the far mass is 2.0 m out for (3.0)(2.0)^2 = 12 kg m^2.

flashcards.meaning: Moment of inertia adds mass times radius squared
flashcards.explain: Moment of inertia is the rotational analog of mass: resistance to angular acceleration. Each piece of mass counts as mass times the square of its distance from the axis, so spreading mass outward raises I fast.

This shifts the rotation axis from the center of mass to a parallel axis a distance d away. The new inertia is the center-of-mass value plus the total mass times d squared, and it works in both directions.

With constant angular acceleration, the angle swept is initial angular velocity times time plus half alpha times time squared. It is the exact rotational copy of x = v_0 t + (1/2)at^2, radians replacing meters.

mcq.prompt: A wheel starts at rest and spins up with a constant angular acceleration of 4.0 rad/s^2. Through what angle does it turn in 3.0 s?
mcq.wrongExplain: 36 rad forgets the factor of 1/2, 12 rad uses alpha times t as if it were an angle (it is actually the final angular velocity), and 6.0 rad comes from (1/2) alpha t, dropping the square on t.

title: Torque drives rotation
lede: Torque is the rotational version of force, and tau = I alpha is Newton's second law spun on its axis.

cards.heading: Torque
cards.body: Torque is force made rotational: tau = r F sin(phi), where r runs from the axis to where the force acts and phi is the angle between r and F. Only the component of force perpendicular to the lever arm turns anything — pushing straight along a wrench handle, through the bolt, produces zero torque. The lever arm r sin(phi) is the perpendicular distance from the axis to the force's line of action.

cards.heading: Second law, rotated
cards.body: Net torque equals moment of inertia times angular acceleration — the exact twin of F = ma. A given torque spins up a flywheel slowly if the flywheel is heavy or its mass sits far from the axis. For problems with a rope over a pulley, apply F = ma to the hanging mass, tau = I alpha to the pulley, and let the no-slip rope connect them: a = r alpha.

cards.heading: Worked example
cards.body: A frictionless pulley is a uniform disk, mass 2.0 kg and radius 0.10 m, with a 1.0 kg mass hanging from the wrapped rope. For the mass: mg - T = ma. For the pulley: I = (1/2)MR^2 = 0.010 kg m^2, and with alpha = a/r the pulley equation gives T = I a/r^2 = 1.0a. Substituting into mg - T = ma: 9.8 - 1.0a = 1.0a, so a = 4.9 m/s^2 and T = 4.9 N. The mass falls at half of g because half the energy budget goes into spinning the disk.

flashcards.explain: Only the force component perpendicular to the lever arm causes rotation, which is where the sine comes from. Maximum torque means pushing at a right angle to r, and pushing along r gives zero.
Net torque equals moment of inertia times angular acceleration. Same torque, larger inertia — slower spin-up, exactly like F = ma with a heavier cart.

flashcards.meaning: Moment of inertia of a uniform disk
flashcards.explain: A uniform solid disk resists spin about its center with half its mass times radius squared. The 1/2 reflects that most of the disk's mass sits well inside the rim, unlike a hoop where it all sits at R.

mcq.prompt: A 24 N force is applied at the rim of a wheel of radius 0.25 m, at an angle of 30 degrees to the spoke (the radius direction). What is the torque about the axle?
mcq.rightExplain: tau = rF sin(phi) = (0.25)(24) sin(30 deg) = 6.0 times 0.5 = 3.0 N m.
mcq.wrongExplain: 6.0 N m treats the force as fully tangential (90 degrees), 5.2 N m uses cos(30 deg) instead of sin(30 deg), and 12 N m divides by sin(30 deg) instead of multiplying.

title: Angular momentum and rolling
lede: Angular momentum L = I omega survives anything except an external torque — and rolling ties spin to travel with v = omega R.

cards.heading: Angular momentum
cards.body: A spinning body carries angular momentum L = I omega, the rotational twin of p = mv, and it changes only under a net external torque: tau = dL/dt. So whenever outside torques vanish or cancel — good bearings, no air, nothing pushing off-axis — L stays fixed no matter how the body reconfigures itself.

cards.heading: Rolling without slipping
cards.body: A wheel rolling without slipping pins its spin to its travel: the contact point is momentarily at rest, so each radian of rotation advances the axle exactly R meters — v = omega R. A roller therefore carries both translational energy (1/2)mv^2 and rotational energy (1/2)I omega^2: for a rolling disk a third of the total is spin, for a hoop half, which is why a hoop loses a downhill race to a disk.

cards.heading: Worked example
cards.body: A skater spins with arms out at I = 4.0 kg m^2 and omega = 2.0 rad/s, so L = 8.0 kg m^2/s. She pulls her arms in, dropping to I = 1.6 kg m^2; conservation forces omega = 8.0/1.6 = 5.0 rad/s — two and a half times faster. Her kinetic energy climbs from (1/2)(4.0)(2.0)^2 = 8.0 J to (1/2)(1.6)(5.0)^2 = 20 J. No law is broken: pulling her arms in against the outward pull takes muscular work, and that work shows up as spin.

flashcards.meaning: Angular momentum of a spinning body
flashcards.explain: Rotational mass times rotational speed, the analog of p = mv. A net external torque is required to change it; with none, the product I omega stays constant through anything.

With no net external torque, angular momentum is fixed. Pulling mass toward the axis lowers I, so omega must rise by the same factor — this is the figure skater's spin-up and the diver's mid-air tuck.

A rolling wheel's contact point is instantaneously at rest, tying the axle's forward speed to the spin rate through the radius. It also means rolling bodies carry translational and rotational kinetic energy together.

mcq.prompt: A diver leaves the board rotating at 2.0 rad/s with moment of inertia 12 kg·m^2 about her spin axis. She tucks, reducing her moment of inertia to 4.0 kg·m^2. What is her new angular speed?
mcq.rightExplain: L = (12)(2.0) = 24 kg m^2/s is conserved, so the new angular speed is 24/4.0 = 6.0 rad/s.
mcq.wrongExplain: 0.67 rad/s applies the inertia ratio backwards, which would make her spin slower after tucking. 3.0 rad/s divides by the average inertia (8.0 kg m^2) instead of the final one, and 2.0 rad/s assumes tucking changes nothing.
